vignette:
Callum is a 21-year-old white European male, currently unemployed and married, who was referred for psychological assessment following what his GP described as a significant deterioration in his daily functioning. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 42, consistent with a probable PTSD diagnosis, arising from a traumatic event involving a family member approximately eight months ago.

The precipitating event occurred when Callum witnessed a severe physical assault on his father. He had arrived home unexpectedly to find his father on the kitchen floor, badly beaten, blood visible across specific parts of his body that Callum cannot now look at without his chest constricting. The image - more photograph than memory, he says, sharp and static and impossible to move past - has lodged itself in a way that ordinary recollection does not. He cannot narrate the event sequentially; when he tries to put it into words, language seems to dissolve. What remains instead are sensory fragments: the particular smell of that room, which returns without warning when he thinks of what happened, and a series of frozen images, as though someone has pressed pause on the worst frames and left them playing on a loop.

In the weeks that followed, Callum found himself unable to tolerate reminders of what he had seen. When people around him made casual comments about family - at the shops, on the street, anywhere - he felt the memory surface immediately, the smell and the images arriving together, and with them a wave of distress that he could not contain. He began avoiding television programmes and films that might depict violence or family harm, and stopped reading the news altogether. These avoidances brought short-term relief but also meant he spent increasing hours in an unstructured, stimulus-poor environment - which, paradoxically, gave the memories more room to intrude. The more he avoided, the less he had processed, and the more raw and immediate the recollections remained.

What frightened him most in those early months was the way his body refused to settle. Sudden movements by others - a flatmate reaching across a table, a stranger gesturing on the street - sent him immediately into a state of high alert, heart hammering, muscles braced. He could not sleep reliably, lying awake rehearsing threats that might not exist, and on several occasions woke mid-flashback, convinced the assault was happening again, in the present tense. He had come to believe that his body was working against him, responding to safety as though it were danger, and this belief that he could no longer trust his own physiology became one of the most destabilising features of his presentation. The sustained threat state, in turn, made him hypervigilant to anything that resembled the original context - people acting in ways he read as suspicious, any unfamiliar movement in his peripheral vision - so that ordinary social environments became minefields he felt compelled to scan constantly.

Callum is not working, and without the structure of employment, his days have become dominated by threat monitoring and avoidance. He will not remain alone in a room or building - the silence feels dangerous, the absence of another person a condition under which something terrible might happen again - and so he organises his entire day around his wife's schedule. This has placed significant strain on their marriage; she has begun to feel less like a partner and more like a safety object, and both of them are aware of this without knowing how to name it. When the distress becomes unbearable, Callum has on several occasions hurt himself physically, describing it as the only way to interrupt the overwhelming feeling - a strategy that briefly disrupts the internal alarm but leaves him afterwards with a deepened sense that he is no longer the person he was. He is certain he is no longer capable of the things that once defined him, and he cannot rely on himself to manage even ordinary situations. These appraisals - of a self that has fundamentally broken - lower his threshold for perceiving threat in the environment, so that even neutral cues now carry a charge they would not previously have held.

Callum came to seek help after his wife found evidence of the self-harm. What he most fears is that he will never recover the person he was before that afternoon in the kitchen. What he most hopes is that someone can explain why his own mind and body have become so foreign to him.
